subject: chemistry
overview: This unit covers the d-block (transition) elements and the f-block (inner transition) elements: their electronic configurations, periodic trends, and characteristic properties such as variable oxidation states, colour, magnetism, catalysis and complex formation. It also covers two important compounds, $K_2Cr_2O_7$ and $KMnO_4$, and the lanthanoid and actinoid series. NEET asks 2-3 questions from this unit almost every year, usually on configurations, unpaired electrons and magnetic moment, oxidation states, lanthanoid contraction and the reactions of $KMnO_4$ and $K_2Cr_2O_7$.

topics.explanation: The d-block occupies groups 3 to 12, where the differentiating electron enters the $(n-1)d$ subshell. The general configuration is $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{1-2}$, with $Pd$ ($4d^{10}5s^0$) as a notable exception. A transition element has an incompletely filled d subshell either in the atom or in one of its common ions. On this definition $Cu$ is a transition element, because $Cu^{2+}$ is $3d^9$. $Zn$, $Cd$ and $Hg$ are not regarded as transition elements, since they are $d^{10}$ both as atoms and in their common $+2$ state. Exceptional configurations arise from the extra stability of half-filled and fully filled d subshells: $Cr$ is $3d^54s^1$ and $Cu$ is $3d^{10}4s^1$. Transition metals are hard, lustrous and good conductors. They have high melting points and high enthalpies of atomisation, because both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons take part in metallic bonding. They occur mainly as oxides, sulphides and carbonates, and iron is the most abundant transition metal.
key_points: There are four series: 3d ($Sc$ to $Zn$), 4d ($Y$ to $Cd$), 5d ($La$, $Hf$ to $Hg$) and 6d ($Ac$, $Rf$ to $Cn$).
$Cr$ $[Ar]3d^54s^1$ and $Cu$ $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^1$ are the key exceptions in the 3d series.
$Zn$, $Cd$ and $Hg$ have full $d^{10}$ shells, are not true transition elements and have low melting points; $Hg$ is a liquid.
Melting point rises to a maximum near $d^5$ in each series. $Mn$ and $Tc$ are anomalously low.
$W$ has the highest melting point among metals.
A high enthalpy of atomisation goes with a high melting point and noble character.
The 4s orbital fills before 3d, but 4s electrons are removed first on ionisation.

formulas.meaning: General outer electronic configuration of d-block elements

topics.neet_tip: Expect assertion-reason or statement questions on exceptional configurations ($Cr$, $Cu$), why $Zn$ is not a transition element, and why melting points are high (d-electrons take part in metallic bonding).
topics.topic: Transition elements: introduction, electronic configuration, occurrence and characteristics

topics.explanation: Ionisation enthalpy increases gradually across the 3d series, because the nuclear charge rises while the added electrons enter the inner d orbitals and shield only partly. The trend is irregular where half-filled or fully filled configurations are disturbed. $Cr$ and $Cu$ have very high second ionisation enthalpies because $d^5$ and $d^{10}$ cores must be broken. $Mn$ and $Zn$ have high third ionisation enthalpies for the same reason. Oxidation states vary because $3d$ and $4s$ electrons have similar energies. The number of oxidation states rises up to $Mn$, which reaches $+7$ in $MnO_4^-$, and then falls; $+2$ is common for most of the series. Atomic radii decrease at first, stay almost constant in the middle, and rise slightly at $Cu$ and $Zn$. Because of lanthanoid contraction, 4d and 5d elements have nearly equal radii ($Zr\approx Hf$). Higher oxidation states are stabilised by $O$ and $F$, for example $Mn_2O_7$ and $CrO_3$.
key_points: $Sc$ shows only $+3$; $Zn$ shows only $+2$.
$Mn$ shows the most oxidation states, from $+2$ to $+7$.
The highest oxidation state of the early elements equals the sum of their $4s$ and $3d$ electrons.
$Cu$ is the only 3d metal with a positive $E^\circ_{M^{2+}/M}$ ($+0.34$ V), so it does not liberate $H_2$ from dilute acids.
$Mn^{2+}$ ($d^5$) and $Zn^{2+}$ ($d^{10}$) are very stable.
$Mn^{3+}$ and $Co^{3+}$ are strong oxidising agents.
$Cr^{2+}$ and $V^{2+}$ are strong reducing agents.
$Cu^+$ disproportionates in water: $2Cu^+\rightarrow Cu^{2+}+Cu$.
The low $E^\circ$ of $Cu^{2+}/Cu^+$ reflects the high hydration enthalpy of $Cu^{2+}$.
Ionic radius decreases as the oxidation state increases.
Lower oxides are basic, intermediate ones amphoteric and higher ones acidic: $MnO$ basic, $Mn_2O_7$ acidic.
topics.neet_tip: NEET frequently asks which element shows the maximum oxidation states, irregularities in ionisation enthalpy (second IE of $Cr$ and $Cu$), and trends in $E^\circ$ values.
topics.topic: Trends in first-row transition elements: ionization enthalpy, oxidation states, atomic radii

topics.explanation: Most transition metal ions are coloured. Ligands split the d orbitals, and a d electron absorbs visible light to jump to a higher d level (a d-d transition); the observed colour is the complementary colour. Ions with $d^0$ or $d^{10}$ configurations, such as $Sc^{3+}$, $Ti^{4+}$, $Cu^+$ and $Zn^{2+}$, are colourless. $MnO_4^-$ and $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$ are $d^0$, yet they are intensely coloured because of ligand-to-metal charge transfer. Ions with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic, and the spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM. Transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts for two reasons: they show variable oxidation states, and they provide a surface on which reactants adsorb and the activation energy is lowered.
key_points: Ion colours: $Ti^{3+}$ purple, $V^{3+}$ green, $Cr^{3+}$ violet, $Mn^{2+}$ pink, $Fe^{2+}$ green, $Fe^{3+}$ yellow, $Co^{2+}$ pink, $Ni^{2+}$ green, $Cu^{2+}$ blue.
$d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless and diamagnetic.
Magnetic moment values: $n=1$ gives $1.73$ BM, $n=2$ gives $2.83$ BM, $n=3$ gives $3.87$ BM, $n=4$ gives $4.90$ BM, $n=5$ gives $5.92$ BM.
Catalysts: $V_2O_5$ in the contact process; $Fe$ in the Haber process; $Ni$ in hydrogenation; $TiCl_4+Al(CH_3)_3$ (Ziegler-Natta) for polythene.
$Fe^{3+}$ catalyses the reaction $2I^-+S_2O_8^{2-}\rightarrow I_2+2SO_4^{2-}$ by switching between $Fe^{3+}$ and $Fe^{2+}$.

formulas.meaning: Spin-only magnetic moment, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons

topics.neet_tip: The most common question gives an ion and asks for its unpaired electrons or magnetic moment. Also expect identification of colourless ions ($d^0$, $d^{10}$).
topics.topic: Colour, catalytic behaviour and magnetic properties

topics.explanation: Transition metals form many complexes for three reasons: their ions are small, they carry a high charge, and they have vacant d orbitals of suitable energy to accept lone pairs from ligands. Examples are $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$, $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$ and $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$. Interstitial compounds form when small atoms such as $H$, $C$, $N$ or $B$ are trapped in the voids of the metal lattice, as in $TiC$, $Mn_4N$, $Fe_3H$ and $VH_{0.56}$. These compounds are usually non-stoichiometric and are neither typically ionic nor covalent. Alloys form readily because transition metals have similar atomic radii (within about 15 percent), so one metal can substitute for another in the lattice. Examples include brass, bronze and stainless steel.
key_points: Complex formation depends on a high charge/size ratio and the availability of vacant d orbitals.
Interstitial compounds have higher melting points than the pure metal.
They are very hard; some borides approach diamond in hardness.
They retain metallic conductivity.
They are chemically inert.
Interstitial compounds are often non-stoichiometric, e.g. $VH_{0.56}$ and $TiH_{1.7}$.
Brass is $Cu+Zn$.
Bronze is $Cu+Sn$.
Stainless steel is $Fe+Cr+Ni$.
Transition-metal alloys are hard and often have high melting points. They do not, in general, melt higher than their component metals.
topics.neet_tip: Statement-based questions check properties of interstitial compounds (hard, high melting point, conducting, non-stoichiometric) and the reasons for complex and alloy formation.
topics.topic: Complex formation, interstitial compounds and alloy formation

topics.explanation: $K_2Cr_2O_7$ is made from chromite ore, $FeCr_2O_4$, in three steps. The ore is fused with $Na_2CO_3$ in air to give $Na_2CrO_4$. This is acidified to give $Na_2Cr_2O_7$. Finally, treatment with $KCl$ gives the orange $K_2Cr_2O_7$. Chromate (yellow) and dichromate (orange) interconvert depending on pH. In acid, dichromate is a strong oxidant ($Cr^{6+}\rightarrow Cr^{3+}$). $KMnO_4$ is made by fusing $MnO_2$ with $KOH$ in air to form green $K_2MnO_4$. The manganate is then disproportionated in neutral or acidic solution, or oxidised electrolytically, to give purple $KMnO_4$. On heating to 513 K, $KMnO_4$ gives green, paramagnetic $K_2MnO_4$ along with $MnO_2$ and $O_2$. $KMnO_4$ is a $5e^-$ oxidant in acid ($\rightarrow Mn^{2+}$) and a $3e^-$ oxidant in neutral or faintly alkaline medium ($\rightarrow MnO_2$).
key_points: Dichromate structure: two $CrO_4$ tetrahedra share one $O$ atom, with a $Cr-O-Cr$ angle of about $126^\circ$.
Manganate and permanganate ions are tetrahedral.
$K_2Cr_2O_7$ is used as a primary standard because it is non-hygroscopic.
$KMnO_4$ is not a primary standard.
$KMnO_4$ is acidified with $H_2SO_4$, not $HCl$, because $HCl$ is oxidised to $Cl_2$.
$KMnO_4$ ($d^0$) is diamagnetic.
$K_2MnO_4$ ($d^1$) is paramagnetic and green.
In acid, $KMnO_4$ oxidises $Fe^{2+}\rightarrow Fe^{3+}$, $C_2O_4^{2-}\rightarrow CO_2$, $I^-\rightarrow I_2$, $H_2S\rightarrow S$ and $SO_2\rightarrow SO_4^{2-}$.
In neutral or faintly alkaline medium, $KMnO_4$ oxidises $I^-\rightarrow IO_3^-$, $S_2O_3^{2-}\rightarrow SO_4^{2-}$ and $Mn^{2+}\rightarrow MnO_2$.
$K_2Cr_2O_7$ is used in leather tanning, volumetric analysis and the chromyl chloride test.
$KMnO_4$ is used as an analytical reagent, as a disinfectant, and for bleaching wool, cotton and silk.

formulas.meaning: Fusion of chromite ore, the first step in making dichromate
Oxidising action of dichromate in acid ($E^\circ=1.33$ V)
Preparation of potassium manganate from pyrolusite
Permanganate in neutral or faintly alkaline medium

topics.neet_tip: Expect questions on preparation steps, the product of heating $KMnO_4$, the change in oxidation state in different media, balanced stoichiometry (e.g. 2 $MnO_4^-$ react with 5 $C_2O_4^{2-}$) and colour or magnetic character.
topics.topic: Preparation, properties and uses of K2Cr2O7 and KMnO4

topics.explanation: The lanthanoids are the 14 elements from $Ce$ (58) to $Lu$ (71). Their general configuration is $[Xe]4f^{1-14}5d^{0-1}6s^2$. $La$ is $5d^16s^2$, $Gd$ is $4f^75d^16s^2$ and $Lu$ is $4f^{14}5d^16s^2$. The principal oxidation state is $+3$, and $Ln^{3+}$ has the configuration $[Xe]4f^n$, with $n=Z-57$. Some elements also show $+2$ or $+4$, usually to reach $f^0$, $f^7$ or $f^{14}$. $Ce^{4+}$ ($f^0$) is a good oxidant. $Eu^{2+}$ ($f^7$) and $Yb^{2+}$ ($f^{14}$) are reductants. $Tb^{4+}$ is $f^7$. Lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and $Ln^{3+}$ ionic radii from $La$ to $Lu$. It arises because 4f electrons shield the increasing nuclear charge poorly. Its consequences are that 4d and 5d elements have almost the same radii ($Zr$ 160 pm, $Hf$ 159 pm), lanthanoids are hard to separate, and the basicity of hydroxides decreases from $La(OH)_3$ to $Lu(OH)_3$.
key_points: To count unpaired electrons in $Ln^{3+}$, write $4f^n$ with $n=Z-57$ and apply Hund's rule.
For $n\le 7$, unpaired electrons equal $n$; for $n>7$, unpaired electrons equal $14-n$.
$La^{3+}$ ($f^0$) and $Lu^{3+}$ ($f^{14}$) are colourless and diamagnetic.
Most other $Ln^{3+}$ ions are coloured because of f-f transitions.
$Ce^{4+}$ is an oxidant ($E^\circ_{Ce^{4+}/Ce^{3+}}=+1.74$ V).
$Eu^{2+}$ and $Yb^{2+}$ are reductants.
Lanthanoid contraction makes $Zr$ and $Hf$ nearly identical in size and chemistry.
Hydroxide basicity decreases from $La(OH)_3$ to $Lu(OH)_3$.
Lanthanoids react with $H_2O$ to give $H_2$, with $C$ to give carbides, with $N_2$ to give $LnN$, and with halogens to give $LnX_3$.
Mischmetall is about 95 percent lanthanoid metal and 5 percent $Fe$, with traces of $S$, $C$, $Ca$ and $Al$. It is used in lighter flints and in $Mg$-based alloys for bullets and shells.

formulas.meaning: Quick configuration of a trivalent lanthanoid ion

topics.neet_tip: NEET often asks for the number of unpaired electrons or the magnetic moment of a given $Ln^{3+}$ ion, the cause and consequences of lanthanoid contraction, and stable $+2$ or $+4$ states.
topics.topic: Lanthanoids: electronic configuration, oxidation states and lanthanoid contraction

topics.explanation: The actinoids are the 14 elements from $Th$ (90) to $Lr$ (103). Their general configuration is $[Rn]5f^{1-14}6d^{0-1}7s^2$. $Th$ is $6d^27s^2$ with no 5f electron. Other examples are $U$ ($5f^36d^17s^2$), $Pu$ ($5f^67s^2$), $Am$ ($5f^77s^2$) and $Cm$ ($5f^76d^17s^2$). The 5f, 6d and 7s levels have comparable energies, and 5f orbitals are less deeply buried than 4f orbitals. As a result, actinoids show a much wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids. $+3$ is common, but the early actinoids reach higher states: $Th$ $+4$, $Pa$ $+5$, $U$ $+6$, and $Np$ and $Pu$ up to $+7$. All actinoids are radioactive, and those after uranium are synthetic. Actinoid contraction, from element to element, is greater than lanthanoid contraction because 5f electrons shield even more poorly.
key_points: Actinoids show more oxidation states than lanthanoids because 5f, 6d and 7s energies are comparable.
The maximum oxidation state is $+7$, shown by $Np$ and $Pu$.
$U$ commonly shows $+6$, as in $UO_2^{2+}$ and $UF_6$.
Actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction.
All actinoids are radioactive.
Elements beyond $U$ ($Z>92$) are transuranic and synthetic.
Actinoid chemistry is more complex because of radioactivity and the wide range of oxidation states.
Later actinoids behave more like lanthanoids and show mainly $+3$.
topics.neet_tip: Typical questions compare lanthanoids and actinoids (range of oxidation states, size of contraction, radioactivity) and ask for the maximum oxidation state shown by an actinoid.
topics.topic: Actinoids: electronic configuration and oxidation states

common_traps: Removing 3d electrons before 4s when writing ion configurations. The 4s electrons are lost first, so $Fe^{2+}$ is $[Ar]3d^6$, not $[Ar]3d^44s^2$.
Calling $Zn$ a transition element. $Zn$ has a full $d^{10}$ shell in the atom and in $Zn^{2+}$. $Cu$ is a transition element because $Cu^{2+}$ is $3d^9$.
Assuming every coloured compound owes its colour to d-d transitions. $KMnO_4$ and $K_2Cr_2O_7$ are $d^0$, and their colour comes from charge transfer.
Confusing the products of heating $KMnO_4$. It gives green, paramagnetic $K_2MnO_4$ plus $MnO_2$ and $O_2$, not $MnO$ or $Mn_3O_4$.
Using $HCl$ to acidify $KMnO_4$ in titrations. $HCl$ is oxidised to $Cl_2$, so dilute $H_2SO_4$ is used.
Counting unpaired electrons in $Ln^{3+}$ incorrectly. Beyond $f^7$, unpaired electrons equal $14-n$; for example, $f^8$ has 6 and $f^{10}$ has 4.
Assuming lanthanoids show as many oxidation states as actinoids. Lanthanoids show mainly $+3$; actinoids show a wide range, up to $+7$ for $Np$ and $Pu$.
Assuming atomic radius keeps rising down the group from 4d to 5d. Lanthanoid contraction makes the radii nearly equal ($Zr\approx Hf$).
quick_revision: Transition element: incompletely filled d subshell in the atom or a common ion. $Zn$, $Cd$ and $Hg$ are excluded.
$Cr$ is $3d^54s^1$ and $Cu$ is $3d^{10}4s^1$. High melting points arise because d and s electrons both take part in metallic bonding.
$Mn$ shows the most oxidation states ($+2$ to $+7$). $Sc$ shows only $+3$ and $Zn$ only $+2$.
$Cu$ is the only 3d metal with a positive $E^\circ_{M^{2+}/M}$. $Cu^+$ disproportionates in water.
$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM. $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless and diamagnetic.
Interstitial compounds are hard, high-melting, conducting, inert and non-stoichiometric.
Dichromate is orange in acid and chromate is yellow in base. $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$ takes $6e^-$ to give $2Cr^{3+}$.
$KMnO_4$ is a $5e^-$ oxidant in acid ($\rightarrow Mn^{2+}$) and a $3e^-$ oxidant in neutral medium ($\rightarrow MnO_2$). At 513 K it gives $K_2MnO_4+MnO_2+O_2$.
$Ln^{3+}=4f^{Z-57}$. $Ce^{4+}$ is an oxidant; $Eu^{2+}$ and $Yb^{2+}$ are reductants.
Lanthanoid contraction: poor 4f shielding leads to $Zr\approx Hf$ and decreasing basicity from $La(OH)_3$ to $Lu(OH)_3$.
Actinoids are all radioactive, show a wide range of oxidation states (up to $+7$ for $Np$ and $Pu$), and have a greater contraction than lanthanoids.
